philistia.why: Bible Atlas puts Philistia in Lebanon. The dot now sits on the southern coastal plain, among the five Philistine cities.

edom.why: Bible Atlas puts Edom west of the Arabah, in the Negev. The dot now sits at Bozrah, Edom's capital, in the hills east of the Arabah.

sheba-6.why: Bible Atlas puts Sheba at Addis Ababa, though its own description places it in southern Arabia. The dot now sits at Marib in Yemen, the capital of Saba.

canaan-2.why: Bible Atlas puts the land of Canaan on the same point as the city of Gath. The dot now sits in the middle of the land west of the Jordan.

midian-2.why: Bible Atlas puts Midian on the Sinai side of the Gulf of Aqaba. Most scholars place it in northwest Arabia, east of the gulf, where the dot now sits (near al-Bad').

meshech-2.why: Bible Atlas puts Meshech north of the Caspian Sea. Most scholars identify it with the Mushku of Assyrian records, in central Anatolia (Turkey), where the dot now sits.

ophir-2.why: No one knows where Ophir was (proposals run from Arabia to East Africa and India), so the map shows no dot for it.

seba-2.why: Seba's location is uncertain (Meroë in Sudan, or somewhere in Arabia or East Africa), so the map shows no dot for it.

decapolis.why: Bible Atlas puts the Decapolis at Damascus, though its own description places the district east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee. The dot now sits among its core cities, between Gadara, Pella and Abila.

asia.why: Bible Atlas puts Asia in the middle of Anatolia. In the New Testament Asia is the Roman province along the Aegean coast of Asia Minor, where the dot now sits, between Ephesus, Sardis and Pergamum.

bithynia.why: Bible Atlas puts Bithynia out in the Black Sea. The dot now sits on land in northwest Asia Minor, near its chief cities Nicaea and Nicomedia.

cappadocia.why: Bible Atlas puts Cappadocia down near the Cilician plain. The dot now sits on the Cappadocian plateau of central Asia Minor, near its capital Caesarea Mazaca (Kayseri).

galatia.why: Bible Atlas puts Galatia almost on Lycaonia's point, near Iconium. Galatia took its name from the Celtic Galatians settled around Ancyra (Ankara), where the dot now sits. The Roman province of Galatia also reached south to Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, and scholars differ over which part Paul meant.

syria.why: Bible Atlas puts Syria north of Aleppo, in what is now southern Turkey, at the edge of the land. The dot now sits in central Syria near Homs, between Damascus (the capital of Aram in the Old Testament) and Antioch (the capital of the Roman province in the New).

salmone.why: Bible Atlas puts Salmone in the western Peloponnese of Greece, though its own description calls it the cape at the east end of Crete, modern Cape Sidero, where the dot now sits.

adria.why: Bible Atlas puts Adria in the middle of today's Adriatic Sea. In Paul's day the name also covered the open sea between Crete and Sicily, as Bible Atlas's own description says, and that is where the ship drifted toward Malta; the dot now sits there.

phrygia.why: Bible Atlas gives Phrygia only a latitude. The dot sits in the middle of the Phrygian uplands of west-central Asia Minor, near modern Afyon.

azotus.why: Bible Atlas gives Azotus only a latitude. Azotus is the Greek name of Ashdod, so the dot uses Bible Atlas's point for Ashdod.

chios.why: Bible Atlas gives Chios only a latitude. The dot sits on the island of Chios, off the coast of Asia Minor west of Smyrna.

clauda.why: Bible Atlas gives Clauda (Cauda) only a latitude. The dot sits on the island, modern Gavdos, south of Crete's western end.

lasea.why: Bible Atlas gives Lasea only a latitude. Its own description puts the ruins about five miles east of Fair Havens on Crete's south coast, where the dot now sits.

nile.why: Bible Atlas draws the Nile far up the river in Sudan, over a thousand kilometers south of Egypt. The dot now sits at the head of the delta near Memphis and Cairo.

telassar.why: Bible Atlas draws Telassar in southwest Iran, but Isaiah 37:12 and 2 Kings 19:12 tie it to the people of Eden (Bit-Adini) on the Euphrates in northern Mesopotamia. Its exact site is uncertain, so the map shows no dot.

uphaz.why: Bible Atlas draws Uphaz in central India, but Daniel 10:5 and Jeremiah 10:9 give no location and no one knows where it was (some think it is a variant of Ophir). The map shows no dot.

pelusium.why: Bible Atlas puts Pelusium in the southern Sinai, near the Gulf of Suez. Pelusium (Sin in Ezekiel 30:15) was the border fortress at the eastern edge of the Nile delta, where the dot now sits (Tell el-Farama).

lud-2.why: Bible Atlas puts Lud at Lod (Lydda) in Israel, but Ezekiel 27:10 and 30:5 name a far-off people. Lud may be Lydia in western Turkey or a people in North Africa, so the map shows no dot.

koa.why: Bible Atlas puts Koa on the same point as Persia, in the Iranian highlands. Koa and Shoa (Ezekiel 23:23) are peoples east of the Tigris whose exact lands are uncertain, so the map shows no dot.

shoa.why: Bible Atlas puts Shoa on the same point as Persia, in the Iranian highlands. Koa and Shoa (Ezekiel 23:23) are peoples east of the Tigris whose exact lands are uncertain, so the map shows no dot.

canneh.why: Bible Atlas puts Canneh on the same point as Tel-abib in Babylonia. Canneh (Ezekiel 27:23) is a trading town of uncertain site, so the map shows no dot.

chilmad.why: Bible Atlas puts Chilmad on the same point as Asshur. Chilmad (Ezekiel 27:23) is a trading place of unknown site, so the map shows no dot.

gamad.why: Bible Atlas puts Gamad (Gammad, Ezekiel 27:11) on the same point as Arvad. Its site is unknown, so the map shows no dot.

meshech-tubal.why: Bible Atlas puts the combined name Meshech-Tubal in the same far-northern spot it once gave Meshech. They are two peoples of Anatolia, each linked on its own point, so this combined name has no dot.

magog-2.why: Bible Atlas puts Magog north of the Caspian Sea. Ezekiel names it only as the far northern land of Gog, and its location is debated (Scythians, Lydia and others), so the map shows no dot.

beth-togarmah.why: Bible Atlas puts Beth-togarmah in Armenia. Most scholars identify it with Til-garimmu, the Tegarama of Hittite and Assyrian records, in eastern Anatolia near modern Gurun, where the dot now sits.

hazer-hatticon.why: Bible Atlas puts Hazer-hatticon on the same point as Hamath. Ezekiel 47:16 says only that it lay by the border of Hauran, and its site is unknown, so the map shows no dot.

sibraim.why: Bible Atlas puts Sibraim on the same point as Hamath. Ezekiel 47:16 says only that it lay between the borders of Damascus and Hamath, and its site is unknown, so the map shows no dot.

hamonah.why: Hamonah is a name Ezekiel 39:16 gives to a city of the future; Bible Atlas puts it on a point east of the Dead Sea. The text does not fix its site, so the map shows no dot.

valley-of-hamongog.why: Ezekiel 39:11 puts this valley "east of the sea" in a prophecy about the future. Bible Atlas picks a point east of the Dead Sea, but the text does not fix the site, so the map shows no dot.

valley-of-the-passengers.why: Ezekiel 39:11 puts this valley "east of the sea" in a prophecy about the future (the Plain calls it the Valley of the Travelers). Bible Atlas picks a point east of the Dead Sea, but the text does not fix the site, so the map shows no dot.

hadrach.why: Bible Atlas puts Hadrach on top of Damascus, but Zechariah 9:1 lists them as two places. Hadrach (Hazrach on the Zakkur Stele, Hatarikka in Assyrian records) is thought to be Tell Afis in northern Syria; the dot sits there. Coordinates of Tell Afis from Wikipedia, "Tell Afis" (checked 2026-10-29); the identification is probable, not certain.
